description: We’re AstroGlazers, six students passionate about coding, AI, and space. For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we’ll use NASA data, research, and teamwork to build and test a useful prototype, then present our idea and what we’ve learned.
summary: GUARDIAN is a health assistant for astronauts on missions where a doctor may be minutes or days away. Astronauts choose their mission environment (the ISS, a lunar base, Mars transit, the Mars surface or a spacewalk), and GUARDIAN adapts its advice to that setting's gravity, radiation, communication delay and onboard medical tools. They point to where it hurts on an interactive 3D body, log vitals and mood, and get a color coded status and action plan from an onboard AI assistant that works without contact with Earth. Readings are compared with each astronaut's own preflight baseline, not general Earth ranges. Our AI models also analyze portable ultrasound scans, estimating how well the heart pumps and measuring the jugular vein, which swells as blood shifts toward the head in weightlessness. Live NASA space-weather data and regular mental-health check-ins complete the picture. As crews travel farther from Earth, they will need to recognize and respond to health problems on their own; GUARDIAN is built to help them do that safely.

1. What does the project do, and how does it work?

GUARDIAN is a health assistant for astronauts on missions where a doctor may be minutes or days away. An astronaut picks their mission environment: the ISS, a lunar base, deep-space transit, the Mars surface, a spacewalk, or the preflight baseline on Earth. GUARDIAN then adjusts what it watches for to fit that setting's gravity, radiation and communication delay to Earth.

  • Interactive 3D body: the astronaut clicks the exact spot that hurts, down to the muscle (left shoulder, lower back, right knee), rates the pain, and sees the spaceflight risks for that area and a simple self-check to try.
  • Vitals and triage: heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen and sleep are compared with the astronaut's own preflight baseline, not just general Earth ranges. A rule engine combines them with the pain map and the mission environment into a colour-coded status and decides whether to contact ground support. An AI assistant (Qwen3-8B, running locally with no internet needed) explains the result and writes a step-by-step action plan in plain language.
    • Heart: estimates the ejection fraction (how much blood the heart pumps per beat) from four standard views.
    • Neck: measures the jugular vein. In weightlessness blood shifts toward the head, and this vein is known to swell and, in some astronauts, to develop slowed flow.
  • Space weather and environment: live NASA and NOAA data on solar flares, radiation and Earth events.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • For astronauts: problems are caught earlier. Small changes in heart rate, blood pressure, sleep or pain are easy to miss on a busy mission, and GUARDIAN flags them against each astronaut's own normal before they become emergencies.
  • For the crew medical officer: better decisions under pressure. Most crews have no doctor on board, only a crewmate with medical training. GUARDIAN gives that person a clear status, a step-by-step plan, and measurements from ultrasound scans they couldn't otherwise read.
  • For flight surgeons on Earth: a fuller picture when contact is possible. Instead of a vague description over a delayed link, they receive organised vitals, a precise pain location and measured scan results.
  • For the mission: more independence. On Mars, a question to Earth and its answer can take 40 minutes or more, and contact can drop out entirely. GUARDIAN's triage works without a connection, so the crew can act on their own when they have to.

3. What is the intended impact?

As missions move to the Moon and Mars, crews will spend months far from a hospital with slow contact with Earth. GUARDIAN aims to give them earlier warning of health changes, make better use of the equipment they already carry, and support better decisions about when a problem needs ground support. The same approach could help people in other remote places, such as Antarctic stations, ships and rural clinics.

4. What tools, languages, hardware or software did you use?

  • Website: TypeScript, React and Vite, with three.js for the interactive 3D body (anatomy models from the open-anatomy-3d project, based on BodyParts3D) and Recharts for graphs.
  • Server: Node.js with Express and a SQLite database. Accounts are protected with hashed passwords, AES-256 encryption for stored connection tokens, data kept separate per user, and rate limiting.
    • Heart: a U-Net outlines the left ventricle in four views from the CAMUS dataset (500 patients). Its volumes are measured with the standard biplane method, and a regression model chosen by cross-validation turns them into an ejection fraction. On CAMUS's official 50-patient test set, the estimate was on average 4.7 percentage points from the expert values.
    • Neck: a U-Net outlines the jugular vein, carotid artery and thyroid, trained on the SegThy dataset (16 healthy volunteers). In 4-fold cross-validation, with each volunteer held out once, the vein outline scored a mean Dice of 0.82 against the expert outlines, with a median area error of 6.5%.
    • Who decides what: a rule engine sets the health status and whether to contact ground support; Qwen3-8B explains the result and writes the action steps.
    • Why it's built this way: tested alone on 300 scenarios, Qwen3-8B got the ground-support decision right only 76% of the time. With the rules deciding, that became 100%.
    • When the AI isn't available: the rule engine answers on its own.
  • NASA and space data: DONKI (space weather), EONET (natural events), POWER (environmental data), APOD, NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center, NASA's Lifetime Surveillance of Astronaut Health (LSAH) averages, and the NASA OSDR OSD-575 dataset (Inspiration4 crew blood tests) for personal baselines.
  • Hosting: Docker on a Google Cloud virtual machine, with Caddy providing HTTPS, at astroguardian.us.
  • Hardware: none built. GUARDIAN works with equipment astronauts already have, such as portable ultrasound, pulse oximeters and blood pressure cuffs.

5. How is your project creative?

  • The AI explains, but the rules decide. In our tests the language model on its own made unsafe calls about when to contact ground support. GUARDIAN therefore splits the job: a rule engine makes every safety decision, and the AI turns it into clear, plain-language steps. The AI is useful without being trusted with decisions it got wrong.
  • Point to where it hurts. Instead of choosing from a list, astronauts click the spot on a realistic 3D body, down to the individual muscle: the left shoulder, a quarter of the abdomen, the centre of the lower back.
  • Smarter use of equipment already on board. Portable ultrasound is already used in space, but reading a scan takes training. GUARDIAN's models outline the heart and the jugular vein and turn the image into measurements.
  • The mission changes the advice. The same symptom is handled differently on the ISS, where Earth is a call away, and on Mars, where a question and its answer can take 40 minutes and the crew may have to act alone.
  • Compared with yourself, not the average. Readings are judged against each astronaut's own preflight baseline, using real blood-test data from the Inspiration4 civilian crew.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Mission environment: gravity, radiation and communication delay all differ between the ISS, the Moon, Mars and spacewalks.
  • Physical health: blood shifting toward the head, changes to the heart and blood vessels, bone and muscle loss, and vision changes from Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS).
    • Every result shows whether the data passed quality checks, so an unreliable reading is flagged instead of acted on.
    • The ultrasound models are labelled as research prototypes and their accuracy is reported.
    • GUARDIAN never claims to diagnose; it supports the crew's decisions.
  • Privacy: health data stays in each astronaut's own account and is never shared, and uploaded scans are analysed without being stored.
